| table _time, host, user, old_partner, new_partner
tuning_guidance: Very low expected volume; alert on all occurrences.
investigation_steps: Treat as a live incident.
Verify the new partner server is a legitimate, authorized DHCP server.
response_guidance: Revert immediately if unrecognized; the new partner may already have received replicated lease state.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCP Failover Mode Changed
description: The failover relationship mode (Load Balance vs. Hot Standby) was changed, altering which server actively serves leases under normal conditions.

data_sources.name: DHCP Audit Log
data_sources.description: Failover mode-change events.

detection_logic: Filters failover mode-change events.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> action="failover relationship modified" field_changed="mode"
| table _time, host, user, old_mode, new_mode
tuning_guidance: Confirm against change tickets.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification.
response_guidance: Revert if unauthorized.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCP Failover Load-Balance Percentage Changed
description: The load-balance percentage split between failover partners was changed, shifting which server issues the majority of leases.

data_sources.name: DHCP Audit Log
data_sources.description: Load-balance-percentage change events.

detection_logic: Filters load-balance-percentage change events.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> action="failover relationship modified" field_changed="load_balance_pct"
| table _time, host, user, old_pct, new_pct
tuning_guidance: Low individual severity; correlate with other failover changes before escalating.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification.
response_guidance: Revert if unauthorized.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCP Failover Maximum Client Lead Time (MCLT) Changed
description: The MCLT setting was changed, affecting how long a failover partner can safely extend a lease during a communication-interrupted state before risking a conflict.

data_sources.name: DHCP Audit Log
data_sources.description: MCLT configuration change events.

detection_logic: Filters MCLT configuration change events.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> action="failover relationship modified" field_changed="mclt"
| table _time, host, user, old_mclt, new_mclt
tuning_guidance: Confirm against change tickets.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification.
response_guidance: Revert if unauthorized.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCP Failover Shared Secret Changed
description: The shared secret used to authenticate the failover replication channel was changed, which — while legitimate during scheduled credential rotation — could also indicate an attacker inserting a known secret to enable a rogue partner relationship.

data_sources.name: DHCP Audit Log
data_sources.description: Shared-secret change events (secret value never logged).

detection_logic: Filters shared-secret configuration change events without exposing the secret value.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> action="failover relationship modified" field_changed="shared_secret"
| table _time, host, user
tuning_guidance: Confirm against a documented credential-rotation schedule.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification.
Verify both partner servers were updated consistently.
response_guidance: Rotate again under controlled conditions if unauthorized.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCP Failover Replication Failed
description: A failover replication attempt failed, which can lead to lease-state divergence between partners if not resolved.

data_sources.name: DHCP Server Operational Log
data_sources.description: Replication failure events.

detection_logic: Filters the DHCP Server Operational channel for replication-failure events.
spl:
index=<windows_index> sourcetype="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-DHCP-Server/Operational" EventCode=20291
| table _time, host, partner_server, error
tuning_guidance: Occasional transient failures are expected during network blips; escalate on repeated/sustained failure.
investigation_steps: Verify network connectivity between failover partners.
response_guidance: Restore connectivity and force replication once resolved.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCP Failover Communication Interrupted State Entered
description: A failover relationship entered the COMMUNICATION-INTERRUPTED state, meaning the partners can no longer confirm each other's status — each partner will begin operating with reduced safety margins, and the state itself could be caused by an attacker deliberately isolating one partner (e.g. via firewall changes) as a precursor to a rogue takeover.

data_sources.name: DHCP Server Operational Log
data_sources.description: Failover state-transition events.

detection_logic: Filters failover state-transition events for the communication-interrupted state.
spl:
index=<windows_index> sourcetype="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-DHCP-Server/Operational" EventCode=20256 new_state="COMMUNICATIONINTERRUPTED"
| table _time, host, partner_server
tuning_guidance: Correlate with known network-maintenance windows affecting the link between partners.
investigation_steps: Verify network connectivity.
Check for concurrent firewall/network changes that could have deliberately isolated the partner (correlate with network-change telemetry).
response_guidance: Restore connectivity; if deliberate isolation is suspected, treat as an active incident.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCP Failover Partner Down State Entered
description: A failover relationship transitioned to the PARTNERDOWN state, meaning this server now believes it is solely responsible for the entire scope, no longer honoring the load-balance split — this is the state an attacker would want to force in order to isolate one partner and let a rogue server assume the other partner's role in a split-brain scenario.

data_sources.name: DHCP Server Operational Log
data_sources.description: Failover state-transition events.

detection_logic: Filters failover state-transition events for the partner-down state.
spl:
index=<windows_index> sourcetype="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-DHCP-Server/Operational" EventCode=20256 new_state="PARTNERDOWN"
| table _time, host, partner_server
tuning_guidance: Confirm against known planned maintenance for the partner server.
investigation_steps: Verify the partner server's actual status.
If the partner is not actually down, treat as a probable split-brain/rogue-takeover attempt.
response_guidance: If the transition was manually forced and the partner is healthy, revert immediately and investigate the forcing account.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Manual DHCP Failover State Transition Forced
description: An administrator manually forced a failover state transition (rather than the state changing automatically due to a detected condition), which is the explicit administrative action an attacker would need to force a PARTNERDOWN state and seize sole control of lease issuance.

data_sources.name: DHCP Server Operational Log
data_sources.description: Manually-forced state-transition events.

detection_logic: Filters failover state-transition events flagged as manually forced (as opposed to automatic detection).
spl:
index=<windows_index> sourcetype="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-DHCP-Server/Operational" EventCode=20256 transition_type="manual"
| table _time, host, user, new_state
tuning_guidance: Very low expected volume outside deliberate DR testing/failover drills; alert on all occurrences.
investigation_steps: Treat as a live incident unless confirmed as a planned failover drill
response_guidance: Revert if unconfirmed and investigate the forcing account.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCP Failover Disabled
description: A failover relationship was disabled/deleted, removing high-availability protection for the associated scope(s) and leaving a single point of failure.

data_sources.name: DHCP Audit Log
data_sources.description: Failover relationship deletion events.

detection_logic: Filters failover relationship deletion events.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> action="failover relationship deleted"
| table _time, host, user, partner_server
tuning_guidance: Confirm against decommission/change tickets.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification.
Assess availability risk from losing HA protection.
response_guidance: Recreate if unauthorized.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCP Failover Correlated with Firewall/Network Change to Partner
description: A firewall or network configuration change affecting connectivity to the failover partner occurred shortly before that relationship entered a communication-interrupted or partner-down state, providing strong evidence the isolation was deliberately engineered rather than an organic network issue — a likely precursor to a rogue-takeover split-brain attack.

data_sources.name: DHCP failover state + firewall/network change logs
data_sources.path: Firewall/network change events joined with a subsequent failover state degradation for the same partner pair
data_sources.description: Cross-source correlation.

detection_logic: Sequences a firewall/network configuration change affecting the partner link with a subsequent failover state-degradation event within a bounded window.
spl:
(index=<firewall_index> action="rule_changed" (dest=<partner_ip_placeholder>))
OR (index=<windows_index> sourcetype="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-DHCP-Server/Operational" EventCode=20256 new_state IN ("COMMUNICATIONINTERRUPTED","PARTNERDOWN"))
| eval stage=case(action="rule_changed","1_fw_change", true(),"2_failover_degrade")
| transaction maxspan=30m startswith=eval(stage="1_fw_change") endswith=eval(stage="2_failover_degrade")
| table _time, eventcount
tuning_guidance: Requires correlating firewall change logs against the specific IP pair used for failover replication; high value once tuned.
investigation_steps: Treat as a confirmed deliberate-isolation attempt.
Restore connectivity and verify neither partner has been supplanted by a rogue server.
response_guidance: Full incident response: restore the firewall rule, verify failover state integrity, and investigate the account that made the firewall change.
author: Threat Detection Library

threshold.baseline_condition: firewall/network change affecting partner link -> failover state degradation

title: Unusually High DHCP Lease Creation Volume
description: A scope issued a much higher volume of new leases than its historical baseline in a short window, which can be legitimate mass onboarding (e.g. a large conference/event) or an early indicator of a DHCP starvation attack in progress.

data_sources.name: DHCP Audit Log
data_sources.description: Lease-assignment event counts per scope in a rolling window.

detection_logic: Bins lease-assignment events by scope and flags counts well above the scope's historical baseline.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> action="lease"
| bin _time span=5m
| stats count as lease_count by _time scope
| where lease_count > 50
tuning_guidance: Baseline per scope; some environments (guest wifi, conference rooms) legitimately see high churn.
investigation_steps: Correlate with DHCP-058 (unique-MAC spike) to distinguish onboarding from starvation.
response_guidance: Investigate if unconfirmed and combined with rapid pool exhaustion.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1499.001: OS Exhaustion Flood

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Unusual DHCP Release Volume
description: An unusually high number of DHCPRELEASE messages were received in a short window, which can indicate mass client shutdown/reboot (e.g. VDI pool cycling) or an attacker deliberately releasing leases to manipulate pool availability.

data_sources.name: DHCP Audit Log
data_sources.description: Release event counts per scope in a rolling window.

detection_logic: Bins release events by scope and flags counts above baseline.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> action="release"
| bin _time span=5m
| stats count as release_count by _time scope
| where release_count > 30
tuning_guidance: Baseline per scope; VDI/kiosk environments legitimately see high release volume.
investigation_steps: Correlate with subsequent lease-issuance patterns for the freed addresses.
response_guidance: Low urgency alone.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1499.001: OS Exhaustion Flood

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Same MAC Address Receiving Many Different IPs
description: A single MAC address received an unusually high number of distinct IP addresses within a short window, which is atypical for a single physical device and can indicate a scripted client cycling through addresses (a starvation technique) or a device with a spoofed/randomized MAC repeatedly re-requesting.

data_sources.name: DHCP Audit Log
data_sources.description: Distinct-IP-per-MAC count in a rolling window.

detection_logic: Counts distinct IPs leased to the same MAC in a rolling window.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> action="lease"
| bin _time span=15m
| stats dc(client_ip) as distinct_ips by _time client_mac
| where distinct_ips>=10
tuning_guidance: Expect some legitimate churn from certain virtualization/container hosts that rapidly cycle MACs; tune per environment.
investigation_steps: Identify the physical location/switch port of the source MAC.
response_guidance: Investigate as a potential starvation-tooling indicator.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Many MAC Addresses from Same Source Switch Port/Segment
description: An unusually high number of distinct client MAC addresses were observed requesting leases via the same relay agent/switch port in a short window, which given a single physical port normally serves one or a small number of devices, is a strong indicator of a scripted DHCP starvation tool spoofing many source MACs from one location.

data_sources.name: DHCP Audit Log
data_sources.description: Distinct-MAC count per relay agent/GIADDR in a rolling window.

detection_logic: Counts distinct client MACs per relay agent address in a rolling window.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> (action="discover" OR action="request")
| bin _time span=5m
| stats dc(client_mac) as unique_clients by _time relay_agent
| where unique_clients > 30
tuning_guidance: Requires relay-agent (GIADDR) visibility, which maps to a switch/VLAN rather than an individual port unless switch DHCP snooping telemetry is also correlated; tune per segment's expected device population.
investigation_steps: Correlate with switch DHCP snooping/port telemetry to isolate the physical source port.
Treat as an active starvation attack if confirmed.
response_guidance: Shut down the offending switch port and investigate the connected device.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1499.001: OS Exhaustion Flood

author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCP Starvation: Unique MAC Spike Against Scope
description: The specification's core DHCP starvation indicator: a sharp spike in distinct client MAC addresses requesting/discovering leases against a single scope in a short window, consistent with a scripted tool (e.g. Yersinia, dhcpstarv) rapidly exhausting the address pool by requesting a lease for every possible MAC.

data_sources.name: DHCP Audit Log
data_sources.description: Distinct-client-MAC count per scope in a rolling window.

detection_logic: Counts distinct client MACs generating DISCOVER/REQUEST/lease events per scope in a rolling window and flags counts above a threshold tuned to the scope's normal onboarding rate.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> action IN ("discover","request","lease")
| bin _time span=5m
| stats dc(client_mac) as unique_clients count by _time dhcp_server scope
| where unique_clients > 100
tuning_guidance: Threshold must be tuned per scope size and normal onboarding cadence; provide a baseline-relative variant (percentage above the scope's own trailing 7-day average) as an alternative to a fixed threshold in environments with highly variable legitimate churn.
investigation_steps: Treat as an active starvation attack.
Identify the source (relay agent/switch port) generating the spike.
Check scope free-address count (DHCP-060) for confirmation of impact.
response_guidance: Block the source at the switch/network level immediately; consider temporarily reducing lease time on the affected scope to recover addresses faster once the attack stops.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1499.001: OS Exhaustion Flood

author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCP Starvation: Repeated Allocation Failure
description: A high number of lease-allocation failures (no free addresses available) occurred against a scope in a short window, direct evidence the pool is exhausted and legitimate clients are being denied service.

data_sources.name: DHCP Audit Log
data_sources.description: Allocation-failure event counts per scope in a rolling window.

detection_logic: Counts allocation-failure events per scope in a rolling window.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> action="no address available"
| bin _time span=5m
| stats count as failures by _time scope
| where failures>=10
tuning_guidance: Very low expected false-positive rate; a scope should essentially never legitimately run out of addresses in a well-sized deployment.
investigation_steps: Confirm current free-address count for the scope.
Correlate with DHCP-058 for the likely cause.
response_guidance: Treat as an active availability incident; expand the pool or mitigate the starvation source.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1499.001: OS Exhaustion Flood

author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCP Scope Address Pool Near Exhaustion
description: A scope's free-address count dropped below a low-watermark threshold, whether from legitimate growth, misconfiguration, or an active starvation attack — regardless of cause, this is an imminent availability risk that needs prompt attention.

data_sources.name: DHCP Server statistics
data_sources.description: Periodic scope statistics polling.

detection_logic: Compares free-address count against a percentage-of-total low-watermark threshold.
spl:
| inputlookup dhcp_scope_statistics.csv
| eval free_pct=round((free_addresses/total_addresses)*100,1)
| where free_pct<10
| table scope, free_addresses, total_addresses, free_pct
tuning_guidance: Requires periodic scope-statistics polling (via PowerShell Get-DhcpServerv4ScopeStatistics on a schedule); tune the watermark per scope's growth rate.
investigation_steps: Determine whether the reduction is due to legitimate growth, exclusions/reservations (DHCP-022), or a starvation attack (DHCP-058).
response_guidance: Expand the scope or address the root cause before the pool is fully exhausted.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1499.001: OS Exhaustion Flood

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Multiple Scopes Exhausted Simultaneously
description: Multiple distinct scopes reach near-exhaustion within the same short window, which is highly unlikely from independent organic growth and consistent with a coordinated, multi-scope starvation attack.

data_sources.name: DHCP Server statistics (fleet-aggregated)
data_sources.path: Scope statistics across all monitored scopes
data_sources.description: Cross-scope correlation of near-exhaustion events.

detection_logic: Counts distinct scopes crossing the near-exhaustion watermark within a rolling window.
spl:
| inputlookup dhcp_scope_statistics.csv
| eval free_pct=round((free_addresses/total_addresses)*100,1)
| where free_pct<10
| bin _time span=1h
| stats dc(scope) as exhausted_scopes, values(scope) as scopes by _time
| where exhausted_scopes>=3
tuning_guidance: Very low expected false-positive rate; treat as a fleet-wide incident.
investigation_steps: Treat as a coordinated fleet-wide starvation attack.
Identify the common source across affected scopes.
response_guidance: Full incident response across every affected scope.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1499.001: OS Exhaustion Flood

author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCP Starvation Network-Telemetry Corroboration (Zeek/Suricata)
description: Network-level telemetry independently confirms a high rate of DHCPDISCOVER messages with distinct, often sequential or clearly-spoofed source MAC addresses — a corroborating variant of DHCP-058 for environments with Zeek/Suricata visibility, useful when the DHCP server's own audit log is unavailable, delayed, or itself under attack.

data_sources.name: Zeek dhcp.log / Suricata DHCP eve.json
data_sources.description: Independent, network-tap-based visibility into DHCP DISCOVER traffic.

detection_logic: Counts distinct source MACs generating DHCPDISCOVER messages observed at the network layer in a rolling window.
spl:
index=<network_index> sourcetype IN ("zeek:dhcp","suricata") dhcp_msg_type="DISCOVER"
| bin _time span=5m
| stats dc(src_mac) as unique_macs by _time
| where unique_macs > 100
tuning_guidance: Requires Zeek or Suricata deployment with visibility on the relevant broadcast domain; this library does not claim Windows DHCP logs alone provide this corroboration.
investigation_steps: Cross-reference against DHCP-058 for server-side confirmation.
response_guidance: Same as DHCP-058.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1499.001: OS Exhaustion Flood

author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCP Starvation Distinguished from Legitimate Onboarding Event
description: A supplementary behavioral check distinguishing likely legitimate mass-onboarding (many distinct, plausible vendor-OUI MAC addresses arriving gradually, e.g. a conference) from a likely attack (MACs arriving in rapid, mechanical succession, or with implausible/sequential/randomized OUI patterns).

data_sources.name: DHCP Audit Log
data_sources.description: MAC arrival timing and OUI distribution analysis during a spike.

detection_logic: During a DHCP-058 spike, computes inter-arrival time variance and OUI diversity; flags low-variance (mechanical) arrival patterns as more likely an attack.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> action IN ("discover","request")
| streamstats current=f last(_time) as prev_time by scope
| eval gap=_time-prev_time
| eval oui=substr(client_mac,1,8)
| bin _time span=5m
| stats dc(client_mac) as unique_clients, dc(oui) as distinct_ouis, stdev(gap) as gap_stdev by _time scope
| where unique_clients>100 AND distinct_ouis<=2 AND gap_stdev<1
tuning_guidance: Illustrative heuristic; tune the OUI-diversity and gap-variance thresholds against your own environment's baseline before relying on it to auto-suppress DHCP-058.
investigation_steps: Use as a supporting signal alongside DHCP-058, not a standalone gate.
response_guidance: Escalate DHCP-058 with higher confidence when this behavioral check also fires.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1499.001: OS Exhaustion Flood

author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCP OFFER from Unapproved Server
description: A DHCPOFFER message was observed on the network from a server IP/MAC not present in the approved-DHCP-server allowlist. This is the network-level ground truth for rogue DHCP detection and does not depend on any Windows DHCP Server log — it works even if the rogue server is not a Windows host at all.

data_sources.name: Zeek dhcp.log / Suricata DHCP eve.json
data_sources.description: OFFER messages with server IP/MAC.

detection_logic: Filters network-level DHCP OFFER messages against an approved-server allowlist.
spl:
index=<network_index> sourcetype IN ("zeek:dhcp","suricata") dhcp_msg_type IN ("OFFER","ACK")
| lookup approved_dhcp_servers.csv ip as server_ip OUTPUT approved
| where isnull(approved)
| table _time, server_ip, server_mac
tuning_guidance: Requires network-tap-based DHCP visibility (Zeek/Suricata/DHCP snooping export); this is the highest-confidence rogue-server detection in the catalogue but cannot be produced from Windows DHCP Server logs alone.
investigation_steps: Physically or via switch telemetry locate the device at server_mac.
Isolate it from the network immediately.
response_guidance: Isolate the rogue server; identify every client that may have received an OFFER/ACK from it and treat their network configuration as untrusted until verified.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: New DHCP Server MAC Observed on Network
description: A DHCP server response was observed from a MAC address not previously seen acting as a DHCP server on this network, providing an earlier, lower-confidence signal than DHCP-NET-001's allowlist check — useful in environments without a maintained allowlist.

data_sources.name: Zeek dhcp.log
data_sources.description: Server MAC first-seen baseline.

detection_logic: Compares observed DHCP server MACs against a rolling first-seen baseline.
spl:
index=<network_index> sourcetype="zeek:dhcp" dhcp_msg_type IN ("OFFER","ACK")
| lookup known_dhcp_server_macs.csv server_mac OUTPUT first_seen
| where isnull(first_seen)
| table _time, server_mac
tuning_guidance: High false-positive rate immediately after a new legitimate server is deployed; maintain the known-server baseline lookup.
investigation_steps: Verify the device and confirm business justification.
response_guidance: Escalate to DHCP-NET-001 handling if unconfirmed.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Multiple DHCP Servers Responding Unexpectedly on Same Segment
description: More than the expected number of distinct DHCP servers responded to broadcast DISCOVER messages on the same network segment in a short window, which — beyond a single approved server (and its failover partner, if any) — indicates a rogue server actively racing to win the DHCP handshake against legitimate infrastructure.

data_sources.name: Zeek dhcp.log
data_sources.description: Distinct responding-server count per segment in a rolling window.

detection_logic: Counts distinct responding server IPs per network segment in a rolling window and flags counts exceeding the segment's expected server count (typically 1-2 for a failover pair).
spl:
index=<network_index> sourcetype="zeek:dhcp" dhcp_msg_type="OFFER"
| bin _time span=10m
| stats dc(server_ip) as responding_servers, values(server_ip) as servers by _time segment
| where responding_servers>2
tuning_guidance: Tune the expected-server-count threshold per segment (accounting for legitimate failover pairs).
investigation_steps: Identify which of the responding servers is not on the approved list.
Isolate it immediately.
response_guidance: Isolate the rogue server; assess which clients may have accepted its OFFER.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCP Server Responding on User Access Network
description: A DHCP server response was observed on a segment tagged as a user-access/workstation network, where no legitimate DHCP server should ever be directly reachable (server infrastructure and DHCP servers are typically isolated from general user segments), consistent with a user endpoint running rogue DHCP server software.

data_sources.name: Zeek dhcp.log
data_sources.description: OFFER events joined against a segment-role lookup.

detection_logic: Joins DHCP OFFER events against a segment-role lookup and flags responses on user-access segments.
spl:
index=<network_index> sourcetype="zeek:dhcp" dhcp_msg_type="OFFER"
| lookup segment_roles.csv segment OUTPUT role
| where role="user_access"
| table _time, segment, server_ip
tuning_guidance: Requires a maintained segment-role lookup; very high value once available given how anomalous this is by design.
investigation_steps: Treat as a live incident.
Physically locate the endpoint.
response_guidance: Isolate the endpoint and investigate for rogue-server software (e.g. dnsmasq, a hosted-hypervisor's built-in DHCP server left in bridged mode) and broader compromise.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Rogue IPv6 DHCP Server (DHCPv6) Detected
description: A DHCPv6 ADVERTISE/REPLY message was observed from a server not on the approved DHCPv6 server allowlist, the IPv6 analogue of DHCP-NET-001. IPv6 rogue-server activity is frequently overlooked because organizations focus IPv4-only DHCP monitoring.

data_sources.name: Zeek dhcp.log (v6) / Suricata DHCPv6
data_sources.description: ADVERTISE/REPLY messages with server address.

detection_logic: Filters network-level DHCPv6 ADVERTISE/REPLY messages against an approved-server allowlist.
spl:
index=<network_index> sourcetype IN ("zeek:dhcpv6","suricata") dhcpv6_msg_type IN ("ADVERTISE","REPLY")
| lookup approved_dhcpv6_servers.csv ipv6 as server_ipv6 OUTPUT approved
| where isnull(approved)
| table _time, server_ipv6
tuning_guidance: Requires network-tap-based DHCPv6 visibility.
investigation_steps: Locate and isolate the device.
response_guidance: Same as DHCP-NET-001.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCP Server Not Present in CMDB/Asset Inventory
description: A server responding to DHCP requests does not have a corresponding entry in the organization's CMDB/asset inventory, which — while not conclusive alone — is a useful supplementary signal alongside the approved-server allowlist checks.

data_sources.name: Zeek dhcp.log + CMDB export
data_sources.path: OFFER events joined against a CMDB asset lookup
data_sources.description: Distinct from the AD-authorization-based allowlist in DHCP-NET-001, since a server could theoretically be authorized in AD but not tracked in CMDB, or vice versa.

detection_logic: Joins DHCP OFFER events against a CMDB-sourced asset lookup and flags server IPs with no matching entry.
spl:
index=<network_index> sourcetype="zeek:dhcp" dhcp_msg_type="OFFER"
| lookup cmdb_assets.csv ip as server_ip OUTPUT asset_id
| where isnull(asset_id)
| table _time, server_ip
tuning_guidance: Requires a maintained CMDB export lookup; treat as a secondary corroborating signal alongside DHCP-NET-001 rather than a standalone alert.
investigation_steps: Cross-reference with DHCP-NET-001/DHCP-AD-001 before escalating.
response_guidance: Investigate and add to CMDB if legitimate, or isolate if not.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCP Snooping Violation: OFFER/ACK on Untrusted Switch Port
description: A switch with DHCP snooping enabled logged a DHCPOFFER or DHCPACK arriving on a port configured as untrusted (i.e. not the uplink to the legitimate DHCP server/relay), which the switch itself blocks by design — a direct, switch-enforced confirmation of a rogue DHCP server attempt at the access-layer port.

data_sources.name: Switch DHCP Snooping log
data_sources.description: Untrusted-port OFFER/ACK block events.

detection_logic: Filters switch DHCP snooping violation logs for blocked OFFER/ACK on untrusted ports.
spl:
index=<network_index> sourcetype=<switch_snooping_sourcetype> event="dhcp_snooping_violation" message_type IN ("OFFER","ACK")
| table _time, switch, port, server_mac
tuning_guidance: Requires DHCP snooping enabled on access-layer switches; extremely high confidence when available since the switch already enforced the block.
investigation_steps: Identify the device connected to the flagged port and investigate it directly.
response_guidance: The switch has already blocked the traffic; disable the port and investigate the connected device for rogue-server software.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCP Snooping Binding Table MAC/IP/Port Mismatch
description: A switch's DHCP snooping binding table (which records legitimate MAC-to-IP-to-port bindings learned from observed DHCP transactions) shows a MAC address associated with an IP or port inconsistent with the corresponding Windows DHCP lease record, which can indicate ARP/IP spoofing being used to hijack another device's leased address.

data_sources.name: Switch DHCP Snooping Binding Table + DHCP audit log
data_sources.path: Cross-source comparison of snooping bindings against server-side lease records
data_sources.description: Requires both telemetry sources.

detection_logic: Compares the switch's DHCP snooping binding table against the DHCP server's own lease table for mismatches.
spl:
| inputlookup dhcp_snooping_bindings.csv
| join type=left client_ip [
    | inputlookup dhcp_current_leases.csv
    | rename client_mac as server_recorded_mac
  ]
| where client_mac!=server_recorded_mac
| table client_ip, client_mac, server_recorded_mac, port
tuning_guidance: Requires periodic export of both the switch binding table and the DHCP lease table; low volume once available.
investigation_steps: Treat as a likely IP/ARP spoofing attempt.
Identify the physical device at the flagged port.
response_guidance: Isolate the port and investigate for spoofing/MITM activity.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Competing DHCP OFFERs with Conflicting Gateway/DNS Values
description: Two or more DHCPOFFER messages for the same client transaction contain different gateway or DNS option values, meaning a rogue server is racing the legitimate one and, if it wins, will redirect that client's traffic/resolution.

data_sources.name: Zeek dhcp.log
data_sources.description: Multiple OFFERs for the same transaction ID with differing option values.

detection_logic: Groups OFFER messages by DHCP transaction ID and flags groups with more than one distinct gateway/DNS value.
spl:
index=<network_index> sourcetype="zeek:dhcp" dhcp_msg_type="OFFER"
| stats dc(gateway) as distinct_gateways, dc(dns_server) as distinct_dns, values(server_ip) as servers by transaction_id
| where distinct_gateways>1 OR distinct_dns>1
tuning_guidance: Very low expected false-positive rate; treat as a live MITM attempt.
investigation_steps: Identify which server won the race (the client's actual ACK) and isolate the losing/rogue server.
response_guidance: Isolate the rogue server immediately.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Client Switches DHCP Server Mid-Session
description: A client that had been consistently leasing from one DHCP server begins leasing from a different server, which can be legitimate (failover takeover, planned migration) or indicate a rogue server has begun winning that client's DHCP transactions.

data_sources.name: DHCP lease history
data_sources.description: Compares the current lease's serving DHCP server against the client's recent history.

detection_logic: Compares each lease event's serving server against the same client's server-of-record from its recent lease history.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> action="lease"
| sort 0 client_mac _time
| streamstats current=f last(server_ip) as prev_server by client_mac
| where isnotnull(prev_server) AND server_ip!=prev_server
| table _time, client_mac, prev_server, server_ip
tuning_guidance: Correlate with known failover events (DHCP-FO-###) and planned migrations before escalating.
investigation_steps: Confirm whether the new server is an approved, expected partner.
response_guidance: Investigate as a potential rogue-server takeover if unconfirmed.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: High DHCP DECLINE Volume Against Single Scope
description: An unusually high number of DHCPDECLINE messages (clients reporting the offered address is already in use) were received against a single scope in a short window, which can indicate a decline-flood attack designed to force addresses into a bad/unusable state and exhaust the pool without ever completing a real lease.

data_sources.name: DHCP Audit Log
data_sources.description: Decline event counts per scope in a rolling window.

detection_logic: Counts decline events per scope in a rolling window.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> action="decline"
| bin _time span=5m
| stats count as declines, dc(declined_ip) as distinct_ips by _time scope
| where declines>=20
tuning_guidance: Occasional legitimate conflicts are expected on misconfigured/dual-homed networks; escalate on sustained high-volume patterns.
investigation_steps: Identify the source client(s) generating the declines.
Check for a resulting spike in bad-address entries.
response_guidance: Investigate as a potential decline-flood attack; identify and block the source.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1499.001: OS Exhaustion Flood

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Same Client Repeatedly Declining Many Different Addresses
description: A single client MAC declined an unusually high number of distinct offered addresses in a short window, which is not consistent with a genuine one-off address conflict and strongly suggests a scripted decline-flood tool.

data_sources.name: DHCP Audit Log
data_sources.description: Distinct-declined-IP count per client MAC in a rolling window.

detection_logic: Counts distinct declined IPs per client MAC in a rolling window.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> action="decline"
| bin _time span=5m
| stats dc(declined_ip) as distinct_declines by _time client_mac
| where distinct_declines>=10
tuning_guidance: Very low expected false-positive rate for a genuine client.
investigation_steps: Physically locate the source device.
response_guidance: Isolate the source device.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1499.001: OS Exhaustion Flood

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Rapid Growth of Bad-Address Table
description: The count of addresses marked bad (unusable, typically from repeated conflict/decline reports) in a scope grew rapidly, directly shrinking the usable address pool even though the addresses were never actually leased to an attacker.

data_sources.name: DHCP Server statistics
data_sources.description: Periodic bad-address-count polling.

detection_logic: Compares the current bad-address count against its value in the prior polling interval and flags large increases.
spl:
| inputlookup dhcp_bad_address_history.csv
| sort 0 scope _time
| streamstats current=f last(bad_address_count) as prev_count by scope
| eval growth=bad_address_count-prev_count
| where growth>=15
| table _time, scope, prev_count, bad_address_count, growth
tuning_guidance: Requires periodic bad-address-count polling; correlate with DHCP-066/067 for the likely cause.
investigation_steps: Cross-reference with recent decline volume.
response_guidance: Clear the bad-address table once the source is resolved.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1499.001: OS Exhaustion Flood

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Bad-Address Records Cleared
description: The bad-address table was manually cleared, which is a routine recovery action after resolving a decline-flood but could also be used to hide evidence of a prior attack.

data_sources.name: DHCP Audit Log
data_sources.description: Bad-address-table clear events.

detection_logic: Filters bad-address-table clear events.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> action="bad address records cleared"
| table _time, host, user, scope
tuning_guidance: Low individual severity; correlate with DHCP-066/067/068 for context.
investigation_steps: Confirm the underlying decline issue was actually resolved before clearing.
response_guidance: No independent response.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: High DHCP NACK Volume from One Scope
description: An unusually high number of DHCPNACK messages were issued by a scope in a short window, which can indicate address-pool/configuration instability, clients requesting addresses outside a recently-shrunk range, or an attacker-driven client renewal-rejection pattern designed to disrupt connectivity.

data_sources.name: DHCP Audit Log
data_sources.description: NACK event counts per scope in a rolling window.

detection_logic: Counts NACK events per scope in a rolling window.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> action="nack"
| bin _time span=5m
| stats count as nacks by _time scope
| where nacks>=15
tuning_guidance: Correlate with recent scope range/subnet changes (DHCP-014/DHCP-019) as a likely benign cause.
investigation_steps: Check for a recent scope configuration change that could explain the NACK spike.
response_guidance: Investigate if unexplained by a configuration change.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1499.001: OS Exhaustion Flood

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Repeated NACK for Same Device
description: The same client MAC repeatedly received NACK responses, meaning that device is unable to obtain a working lease — worth investigating for connectivity/availability impact regardless of root cause.

data_sources.name: DHCP Audit Log
data_sources.description: NACK event counts per client MAC in a rolling window.

detection_logic: Counts NACK events per client MAC in a rolling window.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> action="nack"
| bin _time span=15m
| stats count as nack_count by _time client_mac
| where nack_count>=5
tuning_guidance: Primarily a hygiene/availability signal; escalate to security only if correlated with other suspicious activity.
investigation_steps: Standard connectivity troubleshooting for the affected device.
response_guidance: Standard availability troubleshooting.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1499.001: OS Exhaustion Flood

author: Threat Detection Library

title: NACK Spike Immediately Following Failover State Change
description: A spike in NACK responses occurs immediately after a failover state transition, consistent with lease-state divergence between partners causing legitimate renewal requests to be rejected — a useful corroborating signal for DHCP-FO-008/DHCP-FO-009's severity assessment.

data_sources.name: DHCP Audit Log
data_sources.description: Failover state-change event followed by a NACK-volume spike.

detection_logic: Sequences a failover state-transition event with a subsequent NACK-volume spike within a bounded window.
spl:
index=<windows_index> sourcetype="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-DHCP-Server/Operational" EventCode=20256
| eval stage="1_failover_change"
| append [
    search index=<dhcp_index> action="nack"
    | bin _time span=5m
    | stats count as nacks by _time scope
    | where nacks>=15
    | eval stage="2_nack_spike"
  ]
| transaction maxspan=15m startswith=eval(stage="1_failover_change") endswith=eval(stage="2_nack_spike")
| table _time, scope, eventcount
tuning_guidance: Correlate with the specific failover relationship and scope affected.
investigation_steps: Verify lease-state consistency between failover partners once connectivity is restored.
response_guidance: Force replication once the underlying failover issue is resolved.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1499.001: OS Exhaustion Flood

author: Threat Detection Library

title: New DHCPv6 Scope or Prefix Delegation Created
description: A new IPv6 scope or delegated prefix was created, the DHCPv6 analogue of DHCP-009, and often overlooked since IPv6 is disabled or unmonitored in many environments while still being enabled at the protocol level.

data_sources.name: DHCP Audit Log
data_sources.description: DHCPv6 scope/prefix creation events.

detection_logic: Filters the DHCP audit log for DHCPv6 scope/prefix creation events.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> action="v6 scope created"
| table _time, host, user, scope, prefix
tuning_guidance: Confirm against change tickets; especially scrutinize in environments believed to be IPv4-only, where any DHCPv6 activity is itself anomalous.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification.
Verify IPv6 is intentionally deployed in this environment.
response_guidance: Remove if unauthorized or unexpected.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCPv6 DNS Server Option Changed
description: The DHCPv6 DNS Recursive Name Server option was changed, the IPv6 analogue of DHCP-DNS-001 — dual-stack clients will use this for IPv6 DNS resolution even if their IPv4 DNS server option is untouched and monitored.

data_sources.name: DHCP Audit Log
data_sources.description: DHCPv6 DNS option value-change events.

detection_logic: Filters DHCPv6 option-change events for the DNS Recursive Name Server option and compares against the approved DNS server allowlist.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> action="v6 option value set" option_name="DNS Recursive Name Server"
| lookup approved_dns_servers_v6.csv new_value AS server OUTPUT is_approved
| where isnull(is_approved)
| table _time, host, user, scope, old_value, new_value
tuning_guidance: Maintain a separate IPv6 approved-DNS-server allowlist; treat with the same urgency as DHCP-DNS-001.
investigation_steps: Same as DHCP-DNS-001, scoped to IPv6-capable clients.
response_guidance: Same as DHCP-DNS-001.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCPv6 Delegated Prefix Changed
description: A delegated IPv6 prefix (used for prefix delegation to downstream routers/subnets) was changed, which can alter address space allocated to entire downstream network segments.

data_sources.name: DHCP Audit Log
data_sources.description: Prefix delegation configuration change events.

detection_logic: Filters prefix-delegation configuration change events.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> action="v6 prefix changed"
| table _time, host, user, old_prefix, new_prefix
tuning_guidance: Confirm against network design change tickets.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification.
response_guidance: Revert if unauthorized.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCPv6 Lease Anomaly: Sudden IPv6 Assignment Activity
description: A sudden onset of DHCPv6 lease activity occurred on a network segment with no prior IPv6 lease history, which can indicate a client (or attacker tooling) enabling IPv6 to bypass IPv4-only network monitoring/security controls.

data_sources.name: DHCP Audit Log
data_sources.description: First DHCPv6 lease activity on a segment with no prior IPv6 baseline.

detection_logic: Compares current DHCPv6 lease activity against a baseline of scopes with zero historical IPv6 activity.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> action="v6 lease"
| lookup dhcpv6_active_scopes_baseline.csv scope OUTPUT was_active
| where isnull(was_active)
| stats count by scope
tuning_guidance: Requires a maintained IPv6-activity baseline; particularly high value in organizations that believe themselves to be IPv4-only.
investigation_steps: Determine whether IPv6 was intentionally enabled and monitor for security-control gaps (e.g. firewall/NDR rules that only cover IPv4).
response_guidance: Investigate and ensure IPv6-aware monitoring is in place if this is intentional; disable IPv6 if not.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Rogue DHCPv6 Server via Router Advertisement Correlation
description: A rogue IPv6 Router Advertisement (RA) with the Managed/Other configuration flags set is observed shortly before or alongside DHCPv6 server activity from an unapproved server (DHCP-NET-005), consistent with an attacker running a combined RA+DHCPv6 spoofing toolkit (e.g. mitm6-style attacks) that uses IPv6 to intercept traffic even in IPv4-primary networks.

data_sources.name: Zeek/Suricata IPv6 RA + DHCPv6 telemetry
data_sources.path: Router Advertisement and DHCPv6 server events correlated by source
data_sources.description: Requires IPv6-aware network telemetry.

detection_logic: Correlates rogue Router Advertisement events with unapproved DHCPv6 server activity from the same source MAC within a bounded window.
spl:
(index=<network_index> sourcetype="zeek:ra" managed_flag=1)
OR (index=<network_index> sourcetype IN ("zeek:dhcpv6") dhcpv6_msg_type IN ("ADVERTISE","REPLY"))
| eval stage=case(sourcetype="zeek:ra","1_ra", true(),"2_dhcpv6")
| transaction src_mac maxspan=5m startswith=eval(stage="1_ra")
| where mvcount(mvdedup(stage))>=2
| table _time, src_mac, eventcount
tuning_guidance: Requires IPv6-aware network telemetry (Zeek/Suricata); this is a well-documented attack pattern (mitm6 and similar tools) worth prioritizing even in IPv4-primary environments.
investigation_steps: Treat as a live MITM incident.
Isolate the source device immediately.
response_guidance: Isolate the device; consider disabling IPv6 network-wide as an interim mitigation if RA Guard/DHCPv6 Guard is not deployed.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCP Dynamic DNS Update Failure Spike
description: An unusually high number of DHCP-initiated dynamic DNS update failures occurred in a short window, which can indicate a DNS server outage, a credential/permission problem, or an attacker interfering with the DHCP-to-DNS update pipeline.

data_sources.name: DHCP Audit Log
data_sources.description: DNS update failure event counts in a rolling window.

detection_logic: Counts DNS update failure events in a rolling window.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> action="dns update failed"
| bin _time span=15m
| stats count as failures by _time host
| where failures>=20
tuning_guidance: Correlate with DNS server health/availability before escalating to security.
investigation_steps: Check DNS server availability and the DHCP server's update credentials.
response_guidance: Restore DNS connectivity/credentials.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: DNS A/PTR Record Mismatch Following DHCP Lease
description: A DHCP-driven dynamic DNS update resulted in an A record whose corresponding PTR record points to a different hostname, which can indicate a race condition, a stale record, or an attacker manipulating DNS to misattribute an IP to the wrong hostname for phishing/spoofing purposes.

data_sources.name: DHCP audit log + DNS zone data
data_sources.path: DHCP-driven A record updates cross-referenced against the corresponding PTR record
data_sources.description: Requires DNS zone data in addition to DHCP audit logs.

detection_logic: Compares the hostname in a DHCP-driven DNS A-record update against the hostname currently in the PTR record for the same IP.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> action="dns update" record_type="A"
| lookup dns_ptr_records.csv client_ip OUTPUT ptr_hostname
| where hostname!=ptr_hostname
| table _time, hostname, client_ip, ptr_hostname
tuning_guidance: Some mismatch is expected transiently during lease churn; escalate on sustained/repeated mismatches for the same IP.
investigation_steps: Verify which hostname legitimately owns the IP and correct the stale record
response_guidance: Correct the DNS records and investigate if the mismatch recurs.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCP DNS Update Unexpectedly Overwrites Critical Hostname
description: A DHCP-driven dynamic DNS update modified the A record for a hostname tagged as critical infrastructure (e.g. a domain controller, identity provider, or security-tooling console), which — since applications and users trust DNS names, not raw IPs — could redirect connections intended for that critical service to an attacker-controlled host.

data_sources.name: DHCP audit log
data_sources.description: DNS update events joined against a critical-hostname lookup.

detection_logic: Joins DHCP-driven DNS update events against a critical-hostname lookup.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> action="dns update" record_type="A"
| lookup critical_hostnames.csv hostname OUTPUT is_critical
| where is_critical=1
| table _time, hostname, old_ip, new_ip
tuning_guidance: Requires a maintained critical-hostname lookup (DCs, IdPs, SIEM/EDR consoles, etc.); critical infrastructure should generally use static DNS entries rather than DHCP-driven dynamic updates in the first place — this detection also surfaces that misconfiguration.
investigation_steps: Treat as a live incident.
Verify the new IP is legitimate for this hostname.
response_guidance: Revert immediately if unauthorized; consider moving this hostname to a static DNS record to prevent recurrence.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: DNS Record Deleted by DHCP
description: DHCP deleted a DNS record (typically on lease expiration, per its aging/scavenging configuration), which is routine cleanup but worth monitoring in volume for unexpected scavenging-configuration changes.

data_sources.name: DHCP Audit Log
data_sources.description: DNS record deletion events.

detection_logic: Filters DHCP-driven DNS record deletion events.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> action="dns record deleted"
| table _time, hostname
tuning_guidance: Not independently alertable at scale; escalate only on high-volume or critical-hostname deletions.
investigation_steps: Cross-reference against DHCP-DNS-009 for bulk-deletion patterns.
response_guidance: No independent response.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Unexpected Volume of DNS Records Deleted by DHCP
description: A large number of DNS records were deleted by DHCP scavenging/aging in a short window, which — beyond normal lease-expiration cleanup volume — can indicate a scavenging-configuration attack designed to mass-delete DNS records as a denial-of-service against name resolution.

data_sources.name: DHCP Audit Log
data_sources.description: DNS record deletion event counts in a rolling window.

detection_logic: Counts DHCP-driven DNS record deletion events in a rolling window.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> action="dns record deleted"
| bin _time span=15m
| stats count as deletions by _time host
| where deletions>=50
tuning_guidance: Correlate with the scheduled scavenging interval; a large batch at the expected scavenging time is likely benign.
investigation_steps: Verify against the DNS scavenging schedule.
Check for a recent scavenging-interval configuration change.
response_guidance: Investigate if occurring outside the expected scavenging schedule.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCP DNS Update Ownership Unexpectedly Changed
description: The DNS record's registered owner (the security principal permitted to update it, tracked via the DnsProperty/dnsTombstoned mechanism in AD-integrated zones) changed unexpectedly, which can allow a different account/device to subsequently update or delete the record.

data_sources.name: DNS Server audit log
data_sources.description: Record ownership change events.

detection_logic: Filters DNS record ownership-change events.
spl:
index=<dns_index> sourcetype=<dns_audit_sourcetype> action="record owner changed"
| table _time, hostname, old_owner, new_owner
tuning_guidance: Low volume; correlate with a legitimate device-replacement scenario before escalating.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification for the ownership change.
response_guidance: Revert if unauthorized.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCP DNS Update Security Setting Changed
description: The DHCP server's dynamic-DNS-update security setting was changed (e.g. from 'always dynamically update DNS records with secure updates only' to a less-secure mode allowing unsecured/unauthenticated updates), which weakens the trust model for the entire DNS zone this server updates.

data_sources.name: DHCP Audit Log
data_sources.description: Dynamic-DNS-update security configuration change events.

detection_logic: Filters DNS-update security configuration change events for a weakening transition.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> action="dns update settings changed"
| table _time, host, user, old_setting, new_setting
tuning_guidance: Very low expected volume; alert on all occurrences moving to a less-secure setting.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification immediately.
response_guidance: Revert to secure-updates-only if unauthorized.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1556: Modify Authentication Process

author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCP DNS Update Credential/Service Account Changed
description: The DNS Dynamic Update Credentials (the account DHCP uses to perform secure DNS updates on behalf of clients) were changed, without exposing the credential value itself.

data_sources.name: DHCP Audit Log
data_sources.description: DNS update credential-change events (credential value never logged).

detection_logic: Filters DNS-update-credential configuration change events without exposing the secret value.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> action="dns update credentials changed"
| table _time, host, user, new_account
tuning_guidance: Confirm against a documented credential-rotation schedule.
investigation_steps: Verify the new account is appropriately scoped and not over-privileged.
response_guidance: Rotate again under controlled conditions if unauthorized.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: First-Seen DHCP PowerShell Administrator
description: An account not previously seen running DHCP-module PowerShell cmdlets (Add-DhcpServer*/Set-DhcpServer*/Remove-DhcpServer*) executed one for the first time, worth baseline-tracking given how much administrative capability the DHCP PowerShell module exposes.

data_sources.name: PowerShell Script Block Logging
data_sources.description: Script block events referencing Dhcp cmdlets, joined against a first-seen-administrator baseline.

detection_logic: Filters PowerShell script block events referencing DHCP cmdlets and joins against a first-seen-user baseline.
spl:
index=<windows_index> sourcetype="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational" EventCode=4104 command_line="*Dhcp*"
| lookup dhcp_ps_admins_baseline.csv user OUTPUT first_seen
| where isnull(first_seen)
| table _time, host, user, command_line
tuning_guidance: Requires PowerShell Script Block Logging enabled; expect false positives immediately after onboarding a new DHCP administrator.
investigation_steps: Confirm the account's role and business justification.
response_guidance: Investigate if unconfirmed.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCP PowerShell Administration from Non-Management Host
description: DHCP-module PowerShell cmdlets were executed from a source host outside the expected set of DHCP/AD administration workstations.

data_sources.name: PowerShell Script Block Logging
data_sources.description: DHCP cmdlet execution joined against an expected-management-host lookup.

detection_logic: Joins DHCP cmdlet execution events against a lookup of expected management hosts.
spl:
index=<windows_index> sourcetype="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational" EventCode=4104 command_line="*Dhcp*"
| lookup dhcp_mgmt_hosts.csv host OUTPUT is_expected
| where isnull(is_expected)
| table _time, host, user, command_line
tuning_guidance: Maintain the expected-management-host lookup.
investigation_steps: Confirm the source host is an approved administration workstation.
response_guidance: Investigate if unconfirmed.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Encoded PowerShell Command Manipulating DHCP
description: A base64-encoded (-EncodedCommand) PowerShell invocation was used to run DHCP-module cmdlets, which is a well-known technique to obscure command content from casual log review and a strong indicator of scripted/automated attack tooling rather than interactive administration.

data_sources.name: PowerShell Script Block Logging + Process Creation
data_sources.description: Encoded command invocations, decoded where possible, referencing DHCP cmdlets.

detection_logic: Filters process-creation/script-block events for -EncodedCommand/-e usage where the decoded content references DHCP cmdlets.
spl:
index=<windows_index> (sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4688) OR (sourcetype="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational" EventCode=4104)
| where match(command_line, "(?i)-e(ncodedcommand)?\s+[A-Za-z0-9+/=]{40,}")
| eval decoded=base64decode(command_line)
| where match(decoded, "(?i)dhcp")
| table _time, host, user, command_line, decoded
tuning_guidance: Very low expected false-positive rate; alert on every confirmed occurrence.
investigation_steps: Decode the full command and identify exactly what DHCP change it made.
Treat as a likely scripted attack.
response_guidance: Treat as a live incident; revert any resulting DHCP changes and investigate the host and account.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1027: Obfuscated Files or Information

author: Threat Detection Library

title: PowerShell Modifying Many DHCP Scopes in a Single Session
description: A single PowerShell session invoked scope-modifying cmdlets (Set-DhcpServerv4Scope, Remove-DhcpServerv4Scope, etc.) against an unusually high number of distinct scopes, consistent with a scripted bulk-attack rather than routine interactive administration.

data_sources.name: PowerShell Script Block Logging
data_sources.description: Distinct-scope-targeted cmdlet invocations per session in a rolling window.

detection_logic: Extracts the -ScopeId parameter from DHCP scope cmdlet invocations and counts distinct values per user/session in a rolling window.
spl:
index=<windows_index> sourcetype="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational" EventCode=4104 command_line="*Dhcp*Scope*"
| rex field=command_line "-ScopeId\s+(?<scope_id>\S+)"
| bin _time span=15m
| stats dc(scope_id) as scopes_targeted by _time user host
| where scopes_targeted>=10
tuning_guidance: Tune out known bulk-configuration automation accounts/scripts.
investigation_steps: Identify the account and confirm against known automation tooling.
response_guidance: Investigate if not attributable to approved tooling.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: DNS or Gateway Option Changed via PowerShell
description: Set-DhcpServerv4OptionValue was invoked with -DnsServer or -Router parameters, the PowerShell-scripted path to the same DNS/gateway-redirection outcome covered by DHCP-DNS-001/DHCP-033 — attackers frequently prefer the scripted path since it bypasses the GUI and can be run remotely via WinRM.

data_sources.name: PowerShell Script Block Logging
data_sources.description: Set-DhcpServerv4OptionValue invocations with DNS/Router parameters.

detection_logic: Filters script block events for Set-DhcpServerv4OptionValue invocations referencing -DnsServer or -Router.
spl:
index=<windows_index> sourcetype="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational" EventCode=4104 command_line="Set-DhcpServerv4OptionValue*"
| where match(command_line, "(?i)-(DnsServer|Router)\s")
| table _time, host, user, command_line
tuning_guidance: Treat with the same urgency as DHCP-DNS-001/DHCP-033; correlate to avoid double-counting the same change captured by both the DHCP audit log and PowerShell logging.
investigation_steps: Same as DHCP-DNS-001/DHCP-033.
response_guidance: Same as DHCP-DNS-001/DHCP-033.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: PXE Boot Options Changed via PowerShell
description: Set-DhcpServerv4OptionValue was invoked targeting options 066/067 (boot server/filename), the PowerShell-scripted path to the same PXE-compromise outcome covered by DHCP-040/041.

data_sources.name: PowerShell Script Block Logging
data_sources.description: Set-DhcpServerv4OptionValue invocations with -OptionId 66 or 67.

detection_logic: Filters script block events for Set-DhcpServerv4OptionValue invocations referencing option IDs 66/67.
spl:
index=<windows_index> sourcetype="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational" EventCode=4104 command_line="Set-DhcpServerv4OptionValue*"
| where match(command_line, "-OptionId\s+(66|67)\b")
| table _time, host, user, command_line
tuning_guidance: Treat with the same urgency as DHCP-040/041.
investigation_steps: Same as DHCP-040/041.
response_guidance: Same as DHCP-040/041.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCP Failover Configuration Changed via PowerShell
description: Add-DhcpServerv4Failover or Set-DhcpServerv4Failover was invoked, the PowerShell-scripted path to the same failover-tampering outcomes covered by the DHCP-FO-### namespace.

data_sources.name: PowerShell Script Block Logging
data_sources.description: Failover cmdlet invocations.

detection_logic: Filters script block events for DHCP failover cmdlet invocations.
spl:
index=<windows_index> sourcetype="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational" EventCode=4104 command_line="*DhcpServerv4Failover*"
| table _time, host, user, command_line
tuning_guidance: Correlate with the corresponding DHCP-FO-### detections to avoid double-counting.
investigation_steps: Same as the relevant DHCP-FO-### detection.
response_guidance: Same as the relevant DHCP-FO-### detection.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCP Server Authorization/Deauthorization via PowerShell
description: Add-DhcpServerInDC or Remove-DhcpServerInDC was invoked, the PowerShell-scripted path to the same authorization-tampering outcomes covered by the DHCP-AD-### namespace.

data_sources.name: PowerShell Script Block Logging
data_sources.description: Authorization cmdlet invocations.

detection_logic: Filters script block events for DHCP authorization cmdlet invocations.
spl:
index=<windows_index> sourcetype="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational" EventCode=4104 command_line="*DhcpServerInDC*"
| table _time, host, user, command_line
tuning_guidance: Correlate with DHCP-AD-001/DHCP-AD-002 to avoid double-counting.
investigation_steps: Same as DHCP-AD-001/DHCP-AD-002.
response_guidance: Same as DHCP-AD-001/DHCP-AD-002.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Legacy netsh dhcp Command Executed
description: The legacy netsh dhcp administration command was executed. In most modern environments where the DHCP PowerShell module is the standard tool, use of the legacy netsh interface is rare and worth extra scrutiny.

data_sources.name: Security 4688 / Sysmon Event ID 1
data_sources.path: Process creation events for netsh.exe with dhcp arguments
data_sources.description: Process command-line telemetry.

detection_logic: Filters process-creation events for netsh.exe invocations with dhcp context.
spl:
index=<windows_index> (sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4688 OR sourcetype=<sysmon_sourcetype> EventCode=1) process_name="netsh.exe" command_line="*dhcp*"
| table _time, host, user, command_line
tuning_guidance: Raise severity when netsh dhcp usage is rare in the environment (per the specification's own guidance); baseline the small number of legitimate legacy-script users.
investigation_steps: Review the full command line for the specific change made.
Confirm business justification for using the legacy interface.
response_guidance: Investigate if unconfirmed.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1059.003: Windows Command Shell

author: Threat Detection Library

title: netsh dhcp Remote Server Administration
description: netsh dhcp was used with the server \\<remote-server> syntax to administer a DHCP server other than the local host, which — combined with the rarity of legacy netsh usage generally — is a stronger indicator worth prioritizing over local-only netsh dhcp activity.

data_sources.name: Security 4688 / Sysmon Event ID 1
data_sources.path: Process creation events for netsh.exe with dhcp server \\\\ syntax
data_sources.description: Process command-line telemetry.

detection_logic: Filters process-creation events for netsh.exe dhcp invocations referencing a remote server.
spl:
index=<windows_index> (sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4688 OR sourcetype=<sysmon_sourcetype> EventCode=1) process_name="netsh.exe" command_line="*dhcp*server*\\\\*"
| table _time, host, user, command_line
tuning_guidance: Very low expected volume; alert on all occurrences given the specification's guidance to raise severity for rare netsh usage.
investigation_steps: Identify the target server and the specific change made.
response_guidance: Investigate if unconfirmed.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1059.003: Windows Command Shell

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Unusual Process Execution on DHCP Server
description: A process from the specification's watch-list (cmd.exe, powershell.exe, reg.exe, sc.exe, wmic.exe, rundll32.exe, certutil.exe, bitsadmin.exe, curl.exe, wget, nc/ncat) executed on a DHCP server, which given DHCP servers should normally run a narrow, predictable process set, is worth baseline scrutiny.

data_sources.name: Security 4688 / Sysmon Event ID 1
data_sources.path: Process creation events on hosts tagged as DHCP servers
data_sources.description: Process-creation telemetry filtered to a watch-list of tools.

detection_logic: Filters process-creation events on DHCP server hosts for a watch-list of tools commonly used in post-exploitation activity.
spl:
index=<windows_index> (sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4688 OR sourcetype=<sysmon_sourcetype> EventCode=1)
| lookup dhcp_servers.csv host OUTPUT is_dhcp_server
| where is_dhcp_server=1
| where process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","reg.exe","sc.exe","wmic.exe","rundll32.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","nc.exe","ncat.exe")
| table _time, host, user, process_name, command_line
tuning_guidance: Requires a maintained DHCP-server-host lookup and tuning against legitimate administrative/patching tooling.
investigation_steps: Review the full command line and parent process for legitimacy.
response_guidance: Escalate severity if this process precedes a DHCP configuration change (DHCP-081).

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1059: Command and Scripting Interpreter

author: Threat Detection Library

title: RDP Login to DHCP Server
description: An interactive RDP session was established to a host tagged as a DHCP server, worth tracking as the entry point for a large share of subsequent DHCP-tampering activity.

data_sources.name: Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Logon Type 10 events on DHCP server hosts.

detection_logic: Filters Logon Type 10 (RemoteInteractive) success events on hosts tagged as DHCP servers.
spl:
index=<windows_index> sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4624 Logon_Type=10
| lookup dhcp_servers.csv host OUTPUT is_dhcp_server
| where is_dhcp_server=1
| table _time, host, user, src_ip
tuning_guidance: Baseline the small set of expected DHCP administrators; escalate for unusual accounts/sources.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification.
Watch for subsequent DHCP configuration changes in the same session.
response_guidance: Investigate if unconfirmed.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1021.001: Remote Desktop Protocol

author: Threat Detection Library

title: WinRM/PowerShell Remoting to DHCP Server
description: A WinRM/PowerShell Remoting session was established to a host tagged as a DHCP server, the most common path for remote scripted DHCP administration (and abuse).

data_sources.name: Security Event Log / WinRM Operational
data_sources.description: WinRM session establishment events on DHCP server hosts.

detection_logic: Filters WinRM session events on hosts tagged as DHCP servers.
spl:
index=<windows_index> sourcetype="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-WinRM/Operational" EventCode=91
| lookup dhcp_servers.csv host OUTPUT is_dhcp_server
| where is_dhcp_server=1
| table _time, host, user, src_ip
tuning_guidance: Baseline the small set of expected automation sources/accounts.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification.
Watch for subsequent DHCP configuration changes in the same session.
response_guidance: Investigate if unconfirmed.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1021.006: Windows Remote Management

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Remote Administrative Access Immediately Followed by DHCP Configuration Change
description: A remote administrative session (RDP, WinRM, or SMB administrative access) to a DHCP server is immediately followed by a DHCP configuration change, correlating the access method with the resulting change for faster investigation.

data_sources.name: Security Event Log + DHCP Audit Log
data_sources.path: Remote-access event joined with a subsequent DHCP configuration change on the same host
data_sources.description: Sequence correlation.

detection_logic: Sequences a remote-access event (Logon Type 10 or WinRM) with a subsequent DHCP configuration-change event on the same host within a bounded window.
spl:
(index=<windows_index> sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4624 Logon_Type=10) OR (index=<dhcp_index> action="*changed" OR action="*created" OR action="*deleted")
| lookup dhcp_servers.csv host OUTPUT is_dhcp_server
| where is_dhcp_server=1
| eval stage=case(EventCode=4624,"1_access", true(),"2_change")
| transaction host user maxspan=30m startswith=eval(stage="1_access") endswith=eval(stage="2_change")
| table _time, host, user, eventcount
tuning_guidance: Useful primarily for investigation/context rather than as a standalone high-severity alert; escalate when the resulting change matches a critical-control detection (DHCP-DNS-001, DHCP-033, DHCP-040, etc.).
investigation_steps: Review exactly what change was made and by what access path.
response_guidance: Standard investigation of the specific resulting change.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: SMB Administrative Share Access to DHCP Server
description: An SMB administrative share (C$, ADMIN$) on a DHCP server was accessed remotely, a common path for deploying tooling or manipulating the DHCP database/configuration files directly at the filesystem level.

data_sources.name: Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Network share access events for administrative shares on DHCP server hosts.

detection_logic: Filters network share access events (Security 5140/5145) for administrative shares on hosts tagged as DHCP servers.
spl:
index=<windows_index> sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode IN (5140,5145) share_name IN ("C$","ADMIN$")
| lookup dhcp_servers.csv host OUTPUT is_dhcp_server
| where is_dhcp_server=1
| table _time, host, user, src_ip, share_name
tuning_guidance: Baseline expected backup/monitoring/patching tooling that legitimately uses administrative shares.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification.
response_guidance: Investigate if unconfirmed, especially if followed by DHCP database file access.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1021.002: SMB/Windows Admin Shares

author: Threat Detection Library

title: PsExec-Style Remote Service Creation on DHCP Server
description: A remotely-created Windows service with characteristics typical of PsExec or similar lateral-movement tooling was observed on a DHCP server (e.g. a randomly-named service with an ephemeral binary path), a common technique for gaining SYSTEM-level command execution ahead of DHCP tampering.

data_sources.name: Security / System Event Log
data_sources.description: Remote service-creation events on DHCP server hosts.

detection_logic: Filters service-creation events (System 7045 / Security 4697) on DHCP server hosts for characteristics typical of remote-execution tooling.
spl:
index=<windows_index> sourcetype IN ("WinEventLog:System","WinEventLog:Security") EventCode IN (7045,4697)
| lookup dhcp_servers.csv host OUTPUT is_dhcp_server
| where is_dhcp_server=1
| where match(binary_path, "(?i)(\\Windows\\Temp\\|\\Users\\Public\\)") OR match(service_name, "^[A-Za-z0-9]{8,16}$")
| table _time, host, user, service_name, binary_path
tuning_guidance: Tune the pattern-matching heuristics against your own environment's legitimate remote-deployment tooling.
investigation_steps: Treat as a likely lateral-movement/persistence attempt.
Investigate the source of the remote service creation.
response_guidance: Remove the service and treat the host as potentially compromised.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1021.002: SMB/Windows Admin Shares

author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCP Registry Configuration Modified Directly
description: A registry key under the DHCP Server's configuration hive was modified directly (e.g. via reg.exe or the registry editor) rather than through the DHCP management console or PowerShell module, which bypasses the normal DHCP audit logging pipeline entirely and is a strong anti-forensics/defense-evasion indicator.

data_sources.name: Sysmon Event ID 13
data_sources.path: Registry value-set events under the DHCP Server service configuration path
data_sources.description: Requires Sysmon registry-auditing configured for the DHCP configuration hive; the specific registry path is version-dependent and should be validated against the actual Windows Server version in use before deployment.

detection_logic: Filters Sysmon registry-modification events scoped to the DHCP Server service configuration path.
spl:
index=<windows_index> sourcetype=<sysmon_sourcetype> EventCode=13
| where match(registry_path, "(?i)\\Services\\DHCPServer\\")
| table _time, host, user, registry_path, new_value
tuning_guidance: Requires Sysmon with a registry-auditing config that includes the DHCP Server key path; validate the exact path against the deployed Windows Server version rather than assuming it is identical across versions.
investigation_steps: Treat as a likely anti-forensics/bypass attempt since it circumvents the normal DHCP audit log entirely.
Cross-reference the changed value against the current effective DHCP configuration.
response_guidance: Treat the host as compromised pending investigation; direct registry tampering of security-relevant service configuration is not a routine administrative path.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCP Database or Backup Path Registry Value Changed
description: A registry value controlling where the DHCP database or its backups are stored was changed directly, which can redirect future backups to a location outside the organization's protected backup path or cause the service to fail to find its database on next restart.

data_sources.name: Sysmon Event ID 13
data_sources.path: Registry value-set events for DatabasePath/BackupDatabasePath under the DHCP Server configuration path
data_sources.description: Version-dependent path; validate before deployment.

detection_logic: Filters Sysmon registry-modification events for the database/backup path values under the DHCP Server configuration path.
spl:
index=<windows_index> sourcetype=<sysmon_sourcetype> EventCode=13
| where match(registry_path, "(?i)\\Services\\DHCPServer\\Parameters") AND match(registry_path, "(?i)(DatabasePath|BackupDatabasePath)")
| table _time, host, user, registry_path, new_value
tuning_guidance: Requires Sysmon registry auditing on the specific value names; validate exact registry paths per Windows Server version.
investigation_steps: Verify the new path is legitimate and still covered by backup/recovery processes.
response_guidance: Revert if unauthorized.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCP Configuration Backup Performed
description: A DHCP configuration/database backup was performed. Routine, but the building block for the higher-priority backup-abuse detections below, since a full DHCP backup can reveal network architecture, reservations, DNS infrastructure, gateways, device identifiers, and PXE infrastructure.

data_sources.name: DHCP Server Admin Log
data_sources.description: Backup events.

detection_logic: Filters DHCP backup events.
spl:
index=<windows_index> sourcetype="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-DHCP-Server/Admin" EventCode=1032
| table _time, host, user
tuning_guidance: Not independently alertable at scale; feed into DHCP-087/088.
investigation_steps: Correlate with the automated backup schedule.
response_guidance: No independent response.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1005: Data from Local System

author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCP Backup Performed Outside Scheduled Window by Unusual Administrator
description: A DHCP backup occurred outside the automated scheduled backup window and was initiated by an account outside the expected DHCP administrator set, consistent with reconnaissance/collection of network architecture detail ahead of a broader attack.

data_sources.name: DHCP Server Admin Log
data_sources.description: Backup events joined against a scheduled-backup-window lookup and an expected-administrator lookup.

detection_logic: Filters backup events outside the scheduled-window lookup where the user is not in the expected-administrator lookup.
spl:
index=<windows_index> sourcetype="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-DHCP-Server/Admin" EventCode=1032
| lookup dhcp_admins.csv user OUTPUT is_expected
| lookup backup_schedule.csv host, _time OUTPUT in_window
| where isnull(is_expected) AND (isnull(in_window) OR in_window=0)
| table _time, host, user
tuning_guidance: Requires both an expected-administrator lookup and a scheduled-backup-window lookup.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification.
Determine where the resulting backup file was stored/transferred.
response_guidance: Investigate as a potential collection/reconnaissance activity if unconfirmed.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1005: Data from Local System

author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCP Configuration Restore Initiated
