description: A DHCP configuration/database restore was initiated, which will overwrite the server's current scopes, reservations, options, and policies with the backed-up version — an unauthorized restore can silently roll back legitimate security-relevant configuration changes (e.g. reintroducing an exclusion or reservation that had been intentionally removed).

data_sources.name: DHCP Server Admin Log
data_sources.description: Restore events.

detection_logic: Filters DHCP restore events.
spl:
index=<windows_index> sourcetype="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-DHCP-Server/Admin" EventCode=1033
| table _time, host, user, backup_source
tuning_guidance: Very low expected volume outside disaster recovery; alert on all occurrences and require a change ticket.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification immediately.
Diff the post-restore configuration against the pre-restore baseline for unexpected reintroductions.
response_guidance: Treat unconfirmed restores as a live incident; the resulting configuration may not reflect intended current state.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1490: Inhibit System Recovery

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Unexpected DHCP Backup File Deletion
description: DHCP backup files were deleted from the backup directory, which — combined with any subsequent destructive activity — removes the ability to recover the server's configuration, consistent with a ransomware-style recovery-inhibition step.

data_sources.name: Security Event Log
data_sources.path: Security (file-system auditing on the DHCP backup directory)
data_sources.description: File deletion events in the DHCP backup directory.

detection_logic: Filters file-deletion events scoped to the DHCP backup directory.
spl:
index=<windows_index> sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode IN (4660,4663) object_name="*\\DHCP\\backup\\*"
| table _time, host, user, object_name
tuning_guidance: Requires file-system SACL auditing on the backup directory; alert on all occurrences.
investigation_steps: Treat as a live incident, especially if correlated with other destructive DHCP activity (DHCP-100+).
response_guidance: Treat the server as compromised and assess whether any off-host backup copies still exist.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCP Configuration Export to Unusual Path or Followed by Network Transfer
description: A DHCP configuration export was written to a location outside the organization's standard backup path, and/or was followed by a network transfer of that file — consistent with an attacker collecting network-architecture detail for exfiltration rather than performing a routine backup.

data_sources.name: DHCP Server Admin Log + network telemetry
data_sources.path: Export events to an unapproved path, optionally joined with a subsequent outbound transfer
data_sources.description: Requires network telemetry for the transfer-correlation half.

detection_logic: Filters export events where the destination path is outside the approved backup-path allowlist, optionally sequenced with a subsequent outbound network transfer.
spl:
index=<windows_index> sourcetype="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-DHCP-Server/Admin" EventCode=1032
| lookup approved_backup_paths.csv export_path OUTPUT is_approved
| where isnull(is_approved)
| table _time, host, user, export_path
tuning_guidance: Maintain the approved-backup-path allowlist; the network-transfer half requires DLP/network telemetry not assumed to be universally available.
investigation_steps: Determine what was done with the exported file.
Check for subsequent outbound network activity from the host.
response_guidance: Treat as a potential collection/exfiltration incident.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1005: Data from Local System
MITRE ATT&CK T1041: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel

author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCP Server Migration or Bulk Configuration Import
description: A bulk configuration import (server-to-server migration, Export-DhcpServer/Import-DhcpServer) was performed, which — like DHCP-088 — can make many changes at once and warrants a diff against the pre-import baseline.

data_sources.name: DHCP Server Admin Log / PowerShell Script Block Logging
data_sources.path: Import-DhcpServer cmdlet invocations or equivalent migration events
data_sources.description: Bulk import events.

detection_logic: Filters Import-DhcpServer cmdlet invocations and equivalent bulk-import events.
spl:
index=<windows_index> sourcetype="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational" EventCode=4104 command_line="Import-DhcpServer*"
| table _time, host, user, command_line
tuning_guidance: Expected during planned server migration; require a change ticket for production imports.
investigation_steps: Diff the resulting configuration against the pre-import baseline.
response_guidance: Revert if unauthorized.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Firewall Rule Change Permits New DHCP Traffic (UDP 67/68)
description: A firewall rule change newly permits UDP 67/68 traffic from a network segment that previously could not reach the DHCP infrastructure, expanding the network's rogue-DHCP attack surface by allowing a new source of DHCP traffic to be relayed or reach the server directly.

data_sources.name: Firewall change log
data_sources.description: Rule-change events for the DHCP protocol ports.

detection_logic: Filters firewall rule-change events referencing UDP 67/68 that widen the permitted source zone.
spl:
index=<firewall_index> action="rule_changed" (dest_port=67 OR dest_port=68) protocol="udp"
| table _time, user, src_zone, dst_zone, dest_port
tuning_guidance: Confirm against network-change tickets for planned DHCP relay expansion.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification for the new path.
response_guidance: Revert if unauthorized.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCP Relay Target (Helper Address) Changed
description: A network device's DHCP relay/helper-address configuration was changed to point at a different DHCP server, which redirects every DHCP request from that relay's segment to the new server — if attacker-controlled, this achieves the same DNS/gateway-redirection outcomes as DHCP-DNS-001/DHCP-033 without ever touching the actual DHCP server.

data_sources.name: Network device configuration/change log
data_sources.path: Router/switch DHCP relay (ip helper-address) configuration change events
data_sources.description: Requires network device change telemetry.

detection_logic: Filters network device configuration-change events for DHCP relay/helper-address settings.
spl:
index=<network_index> sourcetype=<network_config_sourcetype> action="config_changed" setting="ip_helper_address"
| table _time, device, user, old_relay_target, new_relay_target
tuning_guidance: Requires network device change-management telemetry; treat with the same urgency as DHCP-DNS-001/DHCP-033 given the equivalent outcome.
investigation_steps: Verify the new relay target is an approved DHCP server.
response_guidance: Revert immediately if unauthorized.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: MAC/Identity Mismatch Between DHCP Lease and NAC Authentication
description: Where a Network Access Control (NAC) system exists, a DHCP lease's client MAC does not match the MAC that most recently authenticated via 802.1X/NAC on the same switch port, which can indicate MAC spoofing to obtain network access under a different device's identity.

data_sources.name: DHCP audit log + NAC authentication log
data_sources.path: DHCP lease events joined against the NAC system's most recent authenticated MAC per port
data_sources.description: Requires NAC integration.

detection_logic: Joins DHCP lease events against the NAC system's most recent authenticated-MAC record for the same switch port and flags mismatches.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> action="lease"
| lookup nac_port_auth.csv port OUTPUT nac_authenticated_mac
| where client_mac!=nac_authenticated_mac
| table _time, client_mac, port, nac_authenticated_mac
tuning_guidance: Requires NAC system integration; high false-positive rate on ports with multiple legitimate devices (e.g. behind an unmanaged switch or VoIP phone with a daisy-chained PC) unless tuned per port type.
investigation_steps: Verify the port's expected device topology before escalating
response_guidance: Investigate the port and connected device(s) if unconfirmed.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: First-Seen DHCP Option Value
description: An option value not previously observed anywhere in the environment's DHCP configuration was set, a low-confidence but broad-coverage behavioral backstop for the option-level detections above, useful for options not covered by a specific named detection.

data_sources.name: DHCP Audit Log
data_sources.description: Option value-change events joined against a first-seen-value baseline.

detection_logic: Joins option value-change events against a rolling first-seen-value baseline per option ID.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> action="option value set"
| lookup dhcp_option_value_baseline.csv option_id, new_value AS value OUTPUT first_seen
| where isnull(first_seen)
| table _time, host, user, option_id, new_value
tuning_guidance: High false-positive rate immediately after deployment while the baseline builds; most useful as a backstop several weeks into monitoring.
investigation_steps: Cross-reference against the specific named detection for this option ID if one exists (DHCP-DNS-001, DHCP-033, DHCP-036, DHCP-040/041, etc.).
response_guidance: Investigate per the relevant specific detection.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Unusual Number of DHCP Changes per Administrator
description: An account performed an unusually high total number of DHCP configuration changes (across all types) in a short window relative to its own historical baseline, a general-purpose behavioral backstop complementing the more specific per-object-type threshold detections above.

data_sources.name: DHCP Audit Log
data_sources.description: Total configuration-change event count per account in a rolling window.

detection_logic: Counts all configuration-change events by the same account in a rolling window and compares against the account's own trailing baseline.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> action="*changed" OR action="*created" OR action="*deleted"
| bin _time span=1h
| stats count as total_changes by _time user
| where total_changes>=30
tuning_guidance: Baseline per account; automation/service accounts will legitimately exceed a fixed threshold and should be tuned separately.
investigation_steps: Identify the specific changes made and cross-reference against the specific named detections.
response_guidance: Investigate if not attributable to approved automation.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Off-Hours DHCP Administration
description: DHCP configuration changes occurred outside the account's normal working-hours baseline, a low-confidence supplementary signal.

data_sources.name: DHCP Audit Log
data_sources.description: Configuration-change events joined against a per-account working-hours baseline.

detection_logic: Compares configuration-change event timestamps against each account's learned working-hours baseline.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> action="*changed" OR action="*created" OR action="*deleted"
| lookup user_working_hours.csv user OUTPUT normal_start, normal_end
| eval hour=strftime(_time,"%H")
| where hour<normal_start OR hour>normal_end
| table _time, host, user, action
tuning_guidance: Requires a maintained working-hours baseline per account; expect a higher false-positive rate for global/24x7 operations teams.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification.
response_guidance: Low urgency alone; escalate if correlated with other suspicious indicators.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Same Administrator Changing Many DHCP Servers
description: A single account made configuration changes on an unusually high number of distinct DHCP servers within a short window, consistent with a scripted fleet-wide attack or a compromised centralized-management credential.

data_sources.name: DHCP Audit Log (fleet-aggregated)
data_sources.path: DHCP audit log, aggregated across servers
data_sources.description: Distinct-server count per account in a rolling window.

detection_logic: Counts distinct DHCP servers with a configuration change by the same account in a rolling window.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> action="*changed" OR action="*created" OR action="*deleted"
| bin _time span=1h
| stats dc(host) as servers_affected by _time user
| where servers_affected>=5
tuning_guidance: Tune out known fleet-management automation accounts.
investigation_steps: Identify the account and confirm against known automation tooling.
response_guidance: Investigate if not attributable to approved tooling; treat as a potential management-plane compromise.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Same New DHCP Option Value Pushed Across Fleet
description: The same new option value (any option, not just DNS/gateway) was pushed across many DHCP servers in a short window, generalizing DHCP-DNS-002/DHCP-035 to catch fleet-wide pushes of any redirection-capable or otherwise security-relevant option.

data_sources.name: DHCP Audit Log (fleet-aggregated)
data_sources.path: DHCP audit log, aggregated across servers
data_sources.description: Option-change events grouped by option ID and new value across servers.

detection_logic: Groups option-change events by option ID and new value and counts distinct servers affected in a rolling window.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> action="option value set"
| bin _time span=1h
| stats dc(host) as servers_affected by option_id, new_value, user, _time
| where servers_affected>=3
tuning_guidance: Very low expected false-positive rate for a coordinated fleet-wide push outside planned change windows.
investigation_steps: Treat as a fleet-wide incident.
response_guidance: Full incident response across every affected server.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Coordinated DHCP Service Stop or Audit Logging Disable Across Fleet
description: Multiple DHCP servers had their service stopped or audit logging disabled within a short window, which given how rarely these individually-critical events should co-occur across a fleet, is a strong indicator of a coordinated, scripted attack against DHCP infrastructure availability and forensic visibility simultaneously.

data_sources.name: System + DHCP Server Admin Log (fleet-aggregated)
data_sources.path: Service-stop and audit-logging-disabled events, aggregated across servers
data_sources.description: Cross-server correlation.

detection_logic: Counts distinct servers with a service-stop or audit-logging-disabled event in a rolling window.
spl:
index=<windows_index> (sourcetype="WinEventLog:System" EventCode=7036 service_name="DHCP Server" state="stopped") OR (sourcetype="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-DHCP-Server/Admin" EventCode=1042)
| bin _time span=30m
| stats dc(host) as servers_affected, values(host) as servers by _time
| where servers_affected>=2
tuning_guidance: Very low expected false-positive rate; treat as a fleet-wide incident.
investigation_steps: Treat as a confirmed coordinated management-plane compromise.
Restore service and logging on every affected server immediately.
response_guidance: Full incident response spanning every affected server; suspend the acting account fleet-wide.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Bulk Scope/Reservation/Exclusion Destruction Sequence
description: The specification's core destructive-attack sequence: a privileged login is followed by bulk scope deletion, bulk reservation/exclusion tampering, and service/logging impairment within a short window — end-to-end evidence of an attacker using DHCP administrative access to maximize network-availability damage while suppressing evidence.

data_sources.name: DHCP Audit Log + Windows Event Log
data_sources.path: Login, bulk-destruction, and logging-impairment events for the same account within a bounded window
data_sources.description: Full destructive-chain correlation.

detection_logic: Sequences a login event with bulk scope/reservation destruction and a service-stop/logging-disable event for the same account within a bounded window.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> OR index=<windows_index>
(action="scope deleted" OR action="reservation deleted" OR action="exclusion range added") OR (sourcetype="WinEventLog:System" EventCode=7036 service_name="DHCP Server" state="stopped") OR (sourcetype="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-DHCP-Server/Admin" EventCode=1042)
| eval stage=case(action="scope deleted" OR action="reservation deleted" OR action="exclusion range added","1_destroy", true(),"2_impair")
| transaction user maxspan=1h startswith=eval(stage="1_destroy") endswith=eval(stage="2_impair")
| where mvcount(mvdedup(stage))>=2
| table _time, user, eventcount
tuning_guidance: Treat any confirmed occurrence as a severe incident regardless of stated justification; the individual component detections (DHCP-012, DHCP-011, DHCP-AUD-001) should already have alerted.
investigation_steps: This is a confirmed severe incident — engage full incident response immediately.
Assess recovery options from the most recent backup.
response_guidance: Full incident response: suspend the account, restore from backup, and audit the account's entire recent activity across the environment, not just DHCP.
author: Threat Detection Library

threshold.baseline_condition: bulk destruction -> service/logging impairment, same account

title: DHCP/Gateway/DNS Option Poisoning Immediately Preceding Server Reboot
description: A DNS/gateway option change (DHCP-DNS-001/DHCP-033) is followed by a server reboot, which forces all currently-attached leases to renew sooner (via the DHCP server's own restart clearing certain caches) and maximizes how quickly the poisoned option propagates to clients.

data_sources.name: DHCP Audit Log + System Event Log
data_sources.path: Option-poisoning event followed by a server reboot
data_sources.description: Sequence correlation.

detection_logic: Sequences a DNS/gateway option-change event with a subsequent server reboot within a bounded window.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> action="option value set" option_id IN (3,6) OR (index=<windows_index> sourcetype="WinEventLog:System" EventCode=1074)
| eval stage=case(action="option value set","1_poison", true(),"2_reboot")
| transaction host maxspan=30m startswith=eval(stage="1_poison") endswith=eval(stage="2_reboot")
| table _time, host, user, eventcount
tuning_guidance: Very low expected false-positive rate; treat as a live incident.
investigation_steps: Treat as a confirmed attempt to accelerate redirection propagation.
response_guidance: Same as DHCP-DNS-001/DHCP-033 with elevated urgency.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCP Server Rebooted Immediately After Destructive Configuration Changes
description: A server reboot occurred shortly after destructive configuration changes (bulk scope/reservation deletion, audit logging disable), which can help clear in-memory state and complicate incident timeline reconstruction.

data_sources.name: DHCP Audit Log + System Event Log
data_sources.path: Destructive change events followed by a server reboot
data_sources.description: Sequence correlation.

detection_logic: Sequences a destructive configuration-change event with a subsequent server reboot within a bounded window.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> (action="scope deleted" OR action="reservation deleted") OR (index=<windows_index> sourcetype="WinEventLog:System" EventCode=1074)
| eval stage=case(action="scope deleted" OR action="reservation deleted","1_destroy", true(),"2_reboot")
| transaction host maxspan=30m startswith=eval(stage="1_destroy") endswith=eval(stage="2_reboot")
| table _time, host, user, eventcount
tuning_guidance: Correlate with DHCP-098 for the full destructive chain.
investigation_steps: Treat as part of a confirmed destructive incident.
response_guidance: Same as DHCP-098.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: AD Privilege Escalation Leading to DHCP Manipulation
description: The specification's core identity-to-DHCP chain: a privileged AD change (the account is added to the DHCP Administrators group or granted equivalent delegation) is followed by that same account modifying a DHCP option — elevating the individual DHCP-AD-009/DHCP-DNS-001-style detections into a single incident-level view spanning identity and network configuration.

data_sources.name: AD Group Membership Changes + DHCP Audit Log
data_sources.path: Privilege-grant events joined with subsequent DHCP option-change events for the same account
data_sources.description: Full identity-to-network-configuration correlation.

detection_logic: Sequences a DHCP-administrative privilege-grant event with a subsequent DHCP option-change event for the same account within a bounded window.
spl:
(index=<ad_index> sourcetype=<ad_audit_sourcetype> EventCode IN (4728,4732) group_name="DHCP Administrators")
OR (index=<dhcp_index> action="option value set")
| eval stage=case(group_name="DHCP Administrators","1_privilege", true(),"2_dhcp_change")
| transaction user maxspan=2h startswith=eval(stage="1_privilege") endswith=eval(stage="2_dhcp_change")
| table _time, user, eventcount
tuning_guidance: Very low expected false-positive rate; treat as a live incident.
investigation_steps: Treat as a confirmed privilege-escalation-to-network-tampering incident.
Revert both the privilege grant and the DHCP change.
response_guidance: Full incident response: suspend the account, revert the DHCP change, and audit the account's broader AD activity.
author: Threat Detection Library

threshold.baseline_condition: DHCP-admin privilege grant -> DHCP option change, same account

title: DHCP DNS Redirection Followed by Client Resolution Shift
description: A DHCP DNS server option change (DHCP-DNS-001) is followed by clients actually renewing their leases and DNS query telemetry showing those clients now resolving through the new DNS server, confirming the redirection took effect and clients are exposed to the new resolver's responses.

data_sources.name: DHCP audit log + DNS query telemetry
data_sources.path: DNS option change joined with subsequent client DNS queries observed against the new server
data_sources.description: Requires network-level or endpoint DNS query visibility.

detection_logic: Sequences a DHCP DNS option-change event with subsequent DNS query traffic from renewed clients directed at the new DNS server.
spl:
(index=<dhcp_index> action="option value set" option_id=6)
OR (index=<network_index> sourcetype=<dns_query_sourcetype>)
| eval stage=case(action="option value set","1_dns_change", true(),"2_client_query")
| transaction dns_server maxspan=4h startswith=eval(stage="1_dns_change") endswith=eval(stage="2_client_query")
| table _time, dns_server, eventcount
tuning_guidance: Requires network-level DNS query visibility (Zeek/firewall DNS logging); treat as a confirmed incident once corroborated.
investigation_steps: Identify every client that has queried the rogue DNS server.
Assess what malicious responses those clients may have received.
response_guidance: Full incident response: revert the option, force client lease renewal, and treat DNS resolution during the exposure window as untrusted.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCP Gateway Poisoning Followed by New Next-Hop Traffic
description: A DHCP gateway option change (DHCP-033/034) is followed by network flow telemetry showing client traffic actually traversing the new gateway address, confirming a live man-in-the-middle position has been established rather than just configured.

data_sources.name: DHCP audit log + network flow telemetry
data_sources.path: Gateway option change joined with subsequent flow records showing the new gateway as next-hop
data_sources.description: Requires NetFlow/flow-log visibility.

detection_logic: Sequences a DHCP gateway option-change event with subsequent flow records showing traffic transiting the new gateway address.
spl:
(index=<dhcp_index> action="option value set" option_id=3)
OR (index=<network_index> sourcetype=<flow_sourcetype> next_hop=*)
| eval stage=case(action="option value set","1_gw_change", true(),"2_traffic_observed")
| transaction gateway maxspan=4h startswith=eval(stage="1_gw_change") endswith=eval(stage="2_traffic_observed")
| table _time, gateway, eventcount
tuning_guidance: Requires flow-level network telemetry; treat as a confirmed active MITM incident once corroborated.
investigation_steps: Treat as a confirmed live man-in-the-middle position.
Identify every client whose traffic has transited the rogue gateway.
response_guidance: Full incident response: revert the option, isolate the rogue gateway device, and treat all traffic through it as potentially intercepted.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: PXE Compromise Chain: Option Change to Boot to Provisioning Activity
description: The specification's full PXE compromise chain: a DHCP PXE option change (DHCP-040/041) is followed by a client DHCP request from the affected scope, then a TFTP boot-file fetch (DHCP-044), then endpoint telemetry showing new OS/provisioning activity on that client — the complete path from a management-plane change to a compromised pre-OS environment on a real endpoint.

data_sources.name: DHCP audit log + network TFTP telemetry + endpoint boot telemetry
data_sources.path: Full multi-stage correlation across DHCP, network, and endpoint sources
data_sources.description: Requires network TFTP visibility and endpoint telemetry showing post-boot activity.

detection_logic: Sequences a PXE option-change event, a subsequent client DHCP request, a TFTP boot-file fetch, and endpoint provisioning/first-boot telemetry within a bounded window.
spl:
(index=<dhcp_index> action="option value set" option_id IN (66,67))
OR (index=<network_index> sourcetype=<tftp_sourcetype> action="GET")
OR (index=<windows_index> sourcetype=<sysmon_sourcetype> EventCode=1 process_name IN ("setup.exe","imagex.exe","dism.exe"))
| eval stage=case(action="option value set","1_config", action="GET","2_tftp_fetch", true(),"3_provisioning")
| transaction maxspan=4h startswith=eval(stage="1_config")
| where mvcount(mvdedup(stage))>=3
| table _time, host, eventcount
tuning_guidance: Requires network TFTP visibility and endpoint process telemetry in addition to DHCP logs; treat any fully-corroborated instance as a confirmed pre-OS compromise.
investigation_steps: Treat as a confirmed pre-OS compromise of the affected endpoint.
Rebuild the endpoint from known-good media; do not trust its current OS state.
response_guidance: Full incident response: isolate and rebuild the affected endpoint, revert the DHCP option, and audit every other client that may have PXE-booted during the exposure window.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Rogue DHCP Compromise Chain: OFFER to Client ACK to Rogue DNS/Gateway Use
description: The specification's full rogue-DHCP chain: an unapproved server's OFFER (DHCP-NET-001) is followed by a client actually accepting it (ACK observed for that server), followed by that client's subsequent DNS/gateway traffic showing it is now using the rogue server's supplied configuration — proving real client impact rather than just a rogue OFFER that was never accepted.

data_sources.name: Zeek dhcp.log + subsequent DNS/flow telemetry
data_sources.path: Rogue OFFER, client ACK, and subsequent client traffic using the rogue configuration
data_sources.description: Full multi-stage network-level correlation.

detection_logic: Sequences a rogue-server OFFER, a client ACK from the same rogue server, and subsequent client traffic consistent with the rogue-supplied DNS/gateway within a bounded window.
spl:
index=<network_index> sourcetype="zeek:dhcp" dhcp_msg_type IN ("OFFER","ACK")
| lookup approved_dhcp_servers.csv ip as server_ip OUTPUT approved
| where isnull(approved)
| stats values(dhcp_msg_type) as msg_types by client_mac, server_ip
| where mvcount(mvdedup(msg_types))>=2
tuning_guidance: Very high confidence given the full client-acceptance corroboration; treat as a confirmed incident.
investigation_steps: Treat as a confirmed client compromise via rogue DHCP.
Isolate both the rogue server and the affected client.
response_guidance: Full incident response: isolate the rogue server and every client that accepted its configuration, and treat their network settings and subsequent traffic as untrusted until manually corrected.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: DHCP Starvation Leading to Legitimate Client Failure
description: The specification's full starvation-impact chain: a unique-MAC spike (DHCP-058) is followed by scope exhaustion (DHCP-060) and then legitimate clients failing to obtain a lease (DHCP-059/repeated NACKs), confirming the attack actually achieved a denial-of-service against real endpoints rather than just consuming address space with no observed downstream impact.

data_sources.name: DHCP audit log + scope statistics
data_sources.path: MAC spike, pool exhaustion, and subsequent allocation-failure events for the same scope
data_sources.description: Full multi-stage correlation.

detection_logic: Sequences a unique-MAC spike, a pool-exhaustion event, and a subsequent allocation-failure spike for the same scope within a bounded window.
spl:
index=<dhcp_index> action IN ("discover","request","lease","no address available")
| bin _time span=5m
| stats dc(client_mac) as unique_clients, count(eval(action="no address available")) as failures by _time scope
| where unique_clients>100 OR failures>=10
| stats values(unique_clients) as spikes, values(failures) as failure_counts by scope
| where mvfilter(spikes>100)!="" AND mvfilter(failure_counts>=10)!=""
tuning_guidance: Treat any fully-corroborated instance (spike + confirmed failures) as a confirmed active availability incident regardless of source attribution status.
investigation_steps: Treat as a confirmed denial-of-service against network onboarding.
Prioritize source identification and blocking over pool expansion, since expansion alone will not stop an ongoing attack.
response_guidance: Full incident response: block the starvation source, and only after the attack stops consider temporary pool expansion or lease-time reduction to accelerate recovery.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1499.001: OS Exhaustion Flood

author: Threat Detection Library
